 Nov. 3, 2026, 9:30 AM UTC Andrew Leahey Drexel University School of Law Technically Speaking design by Jonathan Hurtarte/Bloomberg Tax Related Stories 
 Withholding Scheme Touches About $740 Million in Tax Refunds Oct. 23, 2026, 2:33 PM UTC IRS Racial Audit Disparities Need Accountability to Be Resolved May 21, 2024, 8:30 AM UTC Search by Topic 
 wage withholdings for tax 
 tax identification numbers 
 tax evasion 
 tax fraud 
 federal tax 
 tax audits 
 tax refunds 
 A new TIGTA report identifies tax preparers who exclusively file returns claiming refunds as presenting a heightened risk of potential fraud or misconduct. This raises a broader question about how the IRS can ensure its methods of identifying suspicious tax preparation actually distinguish likely fraud from legitimate circumstances.
 The IRS owes taxpayers more than a hand-wave assurance that its screening methods can detect unusual behavior. It should be able to demonstrate that those methods identify meaningful risks of misconduct so that the resulting allocation of enforcement resources is defensible.
 The report from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration found that more than 38,000 preparers using noncompliant Preparer Tax Identification Numbers prepared more than 2 million returns during the 2025 processing year. Within that group, nearly 12,000 preparers filed approximately 95,000 returns requesting almost $600 million in refunds. 
 What drew TIGTA’s attention was that all of those returns requested a refund and that each preparer filed only returns requesting refunds. TIGTA implied this is an additional indication of risk, though the report doesn’t establish whether the IRS uses a 100% refund rate to select preparers for investigation. The IRS is, however, developing a data-driven preparer compliance program, making the question of indicators timely.
 And why should a preparer whose clients all expect refunds be considered more suspicious than one with some clients that owe taxes or break even?
 Think of tax fraud broadly as a taxpayer trying to extract money from the government they’re not entitled to. It’s obvious that returns claiming refunds might attract additional attention. But a taxpayer who reports owing $500,000 when their actual liability is $750,000 has understated their taxes by a quarter of a million dollars — without requesting a refund. Another taxpayer might improperly claim a $2,000 refund when they should have owed a small sum.
 Deciding to investigate the latter rather than the former could both leave $248,000 in additional tax revenue uncollected and place the risk of miscalibration on a taxpayer less able to bear the cost of defending themselves.
 Receiving a refund also isn’t particularly unusual among many taxpayer groups. Wage earners often have more tax withheld by their employer than they ultimately owe, and refundable tax credits can produce a refund even for a taxpayer with little or no income tax liability.
 A preparer whose practice happens to serve primarily lower-income wage earning households might legitimately prepare nothing but refund returns. Without accounting for the characteristics of the client population, an unusually high refund rate tells us little about whether a preparer is acting improperly.
 Enforcement targeting isn’t a value-neutral exercise of discretion. If we accept that the tax code will never be perfectly enforced, and that the IRS will never have sufficient resources to investigate every potential instance of noncompliance, then attention to one broad subset of taxpayers or preparers consumes resources that could otherwise be targeting another.
 This doesn’t mean we should ignore smaller instances of fraud or that enforcement needs to be reserved for situations where there is a chance of a substantial adjustment. But enforcement burdens can be significant for taxpayers who have made an honest mistake — or no mistake at all.
 An inquiry can be costly, delay refunds, and require taxpayers with the least resources to defend legitimate positions. When the government chooses where to concentrate those burdens, it is making a policy choice.
 This isn’t a hypothetical concern — we’ve discussed Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research’s finding that Black taxpayers are selected for audit at rates between 2.9 and 4.7 times that of non-Black taxpayers. Enforcement priorities favoring the detection of improperly claimed refundable credits over other types of noncompliance can produce the same result. As such, we should demand enforcement choices be justified on grounds more substantial than ease of detection and a statistical departure from the average.
 The IRS should evaluate preparers against appropriately constructed subpopulations rather than treating unusually high refund rates as suspicious. For example, a preparer who completes returns primarily for wage earners should be compared with others serving similar taxpayers, with differences in client filing status, income, and return volume weighed as additional factors.
 Scale is important, as the significance of a 100% refund rate depends on whether the preparer filed 10 returns or 10,000. Taking TIGTA’s numbers, preparers filed an average of just eight refund returns. Although the report doesn’t establish how evenly those returns were distributed, it at least raises the question of how meaningful a 100% refund rate really is.
 The IRS also should validate its risk indicators against independently established instances of noncompliance. We should be asking whether preparers flagged for high refund rates are more likely to have submitted improper returns than comparable preparers with lower refund rates, rather than asking whether they’re occasionally preparing noncompliant returns.
 Ultimately, the agency should examine whether a particular screening criterion produces disproportionate enforcement burdens for certain taxpayer populations, as well as whether the additional tax recovered from those populations justifies the resources expended. These questions should be answered empirically, before allowing statistical assumptions to play a part in enforcement direction. 
 Andrew Leahey is an assistant professor of law at Drexel Kline School of Law, where he teaches classes on tax, technology, and regulation. Follow him on Mastodon at @andrew@esq.social.
